summary: "Specimens of the Russian poets, vol. 1 (of 2)" by John Bowring is a translated anthology of Russian poetry with preliminary remarks and biographical notices written in the early 19th century. The volume introduces English readers to a then-young Russian literary tradition through translations and critical context. It showcases a broad range of verse—odes, elegies, fables, and songs—while sketching the lives and significance of key poets. The opening of the volume presents a modest preface noting the warm reception of the first edition and the aim of familiarizing English audiences with emerging Russian poetry. A substantial introduction surveys Russia’s rapid intellectual awakening since Peter the Great, outlines major poets and genres (with special praise for Derzhavin and the fabulists), and comments on translation principles—especially preserving original meters. It then offers a concise guide to the Russian language and alphabet, with examples of verse forms to illustrate its musicality. The anthology proper begins with translated poems by Derzhavin (including his celebrated hymn to God and other odes), followed by Batiushkov’s intimate “To My Penates” with explanatory notes, and shorter pieces by Lomonosov and Zhukovsky (such as “The Mariner” and the start of “Æolus’s Harp”), all accompanied by brief footnotes that situate the texts and their cultural references.
